item.title: A Punk Rocker’s Painful Wait for Wheelchair Repairs
item.description:
Even before a car crash left him paralyzed, Will Good and the rest of the Old Edison hadn’t performed much in years. The band used to be a regular part of the Boston band scene, hollering folk punk over the twanging of a banjo and fiddle.

Almost six years ago, the crash left Mr. Good hospitalized with a spinal cord injury. As he recovered, well-wishers brought records to add to his vinyl collection. They sat on his shelf, unplayed. Mr. Good had stopped listening to music, and wouldn’t again for a long time.

“It was a huge part of my life, and I didn’t know how to have a relationship with it,” he said.

This summer, the Old Edison encouraged Mr. Good to play a reunion show. Now 36, he would be behind the microphone again, belting out the band’s songs from his motorized wheelchair.

A month before the performance, his specialized chair broke down.

He quickly found himself in a painful limbo that has become increasingly common for many types of wheelchair users across the country. With many local repair shops being bought out by two national companies, the wait for wheelchair repairs can now stretch into weeks, or months, leading to dangerous health complications.

“I’m losing my mind,” Mr. Good said nine days before showtime. Without use of his chair, he spent most of the month leading up to the reunion performance bedridden, dealing with near-constant pain.

More than five million people in the United States use wheelchairs. Some require complex personalization to accommodate particular injuries or disabilities. When those chairs break down, users can find themselves housebound or bedridden, unable to go to work, to school or to medical appointments.

Wait times for service have ballooned over the last decade. Lengthy health insurance approvals and slow parts shipments play a role in the growing backlog. But the delays also corresponded with two private equity-backed companies devouring smaller competitors.

Numotion and National Seating & Mobility now dominate the U.S. market, according to experts, and have greater reach in some states. For instance, Numotion had 47 percent of the Connecticut market and National Seating & Mobility had 45 percent based on revenue, according to a 2024 report to the Connecticut legislature.

“Private equity entering the space has been dangerous,” said Lynn Worobey, who studies wheelchair use at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine. “It used to be a lot of smaller, kind of mom-and-pop stores that were doing this,” she added, “and they have been kind of scooped up by these larger firms.”

Numotion has acquired at least 25 competitors since it was formed in 2013, out of a merger between two smaller companies, according to a report by disability rights advocates and private equity trackers. National Seating & Mobility has bought up at least 42 other companies since 2013, according to the report.

AEA Investors acquired Numotion in 2018. National Seating & Mobility is now owned by Cinven. Both are private equity firms.

Industry representatives declined to comment on specific market data, though Numotion’s website says the company serves more than half a million wheelchair users. A company spokeswoman, Andrea Barnett, acknowledged in a statement that delays are a serious problem and said her company is working on solutions.

It can be difficult to repair highly personalized health equipment and the process is slowed by many outside factors, said Wayne Grau, executive director at the National Coalition For Assistive & Rehab Technology, an industry trade group. National Seating & Mobility would not comment, but said the company supported Mr. Grau’s statement.

The repair delays have prompted investigations by regulators, lawmakers and the news media, including Mother Jones and NPR. California, Colorado, Maryland, Nevada, Oregon and Washington have enacted wheelchair right-to-repair laws over the past five years.

Connecticut now requires companies to complete repairs within 10 business days, and Massachusetts lawmakers have introduced a similar bill.

Chairs like the one Mr. Good relies on are customized, and often do more than wheel a person from place to place. Mr. Good’s, for example, tilts back so that he can relieve the pressure on his skin. A friend’s loaner that he used in the month before his reunion show didn’t fit him right, causing constant pain. He strained to drive it, and kept slipping out.

As a result, he spent most of his time in bed, agonizing over whether his own chair would be fixed before the performance.

The specialized chairs can cost tens of thousands of dollars, yet they frequently break down. Two surveys, including one of veterans and another of users with spinal cord injuries, indicated that more than half needed repairs over a six-month period.

Long waits can lead to life-threatening problems.

While waiting for his repair, Mr. Good developed a pressure wound, caused by the loss of blood flow and breakdown of tissue. About 60,000 hospital patients die from such injuries each year, according to the Department for Health and Human Services.

In July, four days before his reunion show, Mr. Good spent the afternoon waiting for a message from a repair technician as he sat home by his record collection.

Music has turned from a source of pain to once again provide comfort. Mr. Good said he is listening lately to post-punk emo and the new Busta Rhymes record. He has been to several shows, including a Noah Kahan concert at Fenway Park and a Dropkick Murphys show opened by Haywire, the Boston hardcore punk band.

“I need that connectivity,” Mr. Good said. “I need the outlet. I need the community. I need the reprieve.”

That afternoon in July, a past experience had Mr. Good worried that something would go wrong during his repair appointment. Several years ago, a repairman had shown up with a replacement foot plate for the wrong side of the chair.

So when the technician arrived with a tool kit and a cardboard box and saying there had been a problem, Mr. Good was ready to erupt in fury.

The manufacturer had sent the wrong computer part. But the technician said he had managed to swap it for the right one. After a three-and-a-half week wait, the repair took about 15 minutes.

“I’m so lucky,” Mr. Good repeated afterward. “I’m so lucky.”

A few days later, as planned, the Old Edison performed a Sunday matinee for a crowd that had grown up in Boston’s punk scene. As the band altered some of its songs to fit Mr. Good’s slower pace and new vocal range, the crowd still shook fists in the air and belted out the lyrics along with him.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: International Student Enrollment Plunged. Schools Are Bracing for More Losses.
item.description:
The Trump administration’s crackdown on international students is deepening, as it moves to impose new rules and fees that higher education leaders say are likely to further cut enrollment from abroad, which has already dropped by 15 percent this fall.

The recent actions targeting the roughly 1.1 million international students in the United States would make it harder for them to work in the country and, critics say, discourage them from enrolling in American schools.

Universities have pushed back against a federal proposal last month to charge at least $70,000 for student visa holders to gain access to a popular program that lets them work temporarily in the United States after graduation. The administration would charge an extra $30,000 for STEM graduates to receive extensions in the program, known as Optional Practical Training.

The fees would be charged to colleges and universities, and if that cost is passed to students, many fewer could come to the United States.

“In the beginning of the administration, they were taking a hammer to everything and really shocking the system,” said Daniel Delgado, a former senior Department of Homeland Security official who now works at the Searchlight Institute, a centrist Democratic think tank. “Now we’re seeing them translate that into policy.”

The Trump administration has aggressively targeted international students as part of its broader campaign to restrict immigration, arguing that curbing their enrollment would prevent companies from sidelining Americans, especially amid layoffs in the tech industry.

But the recent actions have drawn sharp criticism from universities and business groups that say the loss of international students would make it harder for companies to hire top talent, hurting the country’s competitiveness. Tech leaders have long said that there are not enough U.S. workers for all of their specialized roles, and that international students help fill those gaps.

.

Dennis Galvan, the vice provost for global engagement at the University of Oregon, said the fee would likely have an “even bigger negative effect” on enrollment. The number of international students at the university had already dropped by about 14 percent compared with 2024, he said.

The Optional Practical Training program is “one of the biggest draws” for foreign students to come to the United States and study at the university, Mr. Galvan said. But the university probably would not be able to cover the program’s costs if the fee was imposed, he said.

Many international students rely on the program before seeking H-1B visas, a small number of which are granted to skilled foreign workers each year. Trump officials have also taken aim at the H-1B program, which they have accused of undercutting Americans.

In August, the administration proposed attaching a steep $103,265 fee for H-1B visas, echoing a move by the president last year that was blocked by the courts. This time, the administration is trying to formalize the fee by using a different legal process.

In September, federal officials proposed ending the 60-day grace period that H-1B and other visa holders have to remain in the country after losing their jobs, essentially making them subject to deportation immediately.

The administration’s efforts are expected to face legal challenges. Some of its policies have already been blocked. On Monday, a federal judge vacated a rule that sought to limit the period that students can remain in the country, an attempt to reverse a policy known as duration of status.

The Department of Homeland Security said the proposals would help protect U.S. workers and the country’s “national identity.”

“Our immigration system is being reformed to serve American citizens, American workers, American families, and preserve our national identity, not rapidly import foreigners who take American jobs, commit crimes, burden our welfare system and erode our cultural and social fabric,” the department said in a statement.

Arizona State University was among dozens of schools that criticized the new fee, saying it could “severely damage international enrollment.” That could even affect students from the United States, the university said, because international students often pay full tuition. Losing them, it added, would weaken its “financial base” and academic programs.

Some students worry that if schools pass on the costs of the new fee to them, they would be unable to pursue work in the United States.

Sandra Ding, a senior at the University of California, Berkeley who came to the school from China, said she could not afford to pay at least $70,000 for work authorization.

“Affording an education here is already a huge burden on my family,” said Ms. Ding, who is studying psychology and cognitive science.

The attempts to overhaul work authorization programs are resurfacing tensions with business groups that have at times clashed with the administration over its immigration agenda. In public comments this month, the Chamber of Commerce and organizations representing tech companies, including Apple and Meta, said the new policies would hurt employers and their ability to recruit workers with critical skills.

Mr. Trump has at times scaled back his restrictive immigration policies after outcry from businesses, raising questions about the future of the latest proposals. But administration officials have also made clear that they will pursue what they say is fraud in visa programs.

Miriam Feldblum, the head of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, a group of university leaders, said the administration had been “flooding the zone” with policies targeting international students.

Her group sued the administration over its dismantling of the duration of status policy. The alliance has also challenged the administration’s attempts to limit the Curricular Practical Training program, which authorizes international students to complete internships and other work experiences while enrolled in school. On Tuesday, a federal judge blocked the administration, for now, from carrying out the policy.

Critics of the efforts say the loss of international students would stifle U.S. economic growth and innovation. Economists have generally found that H-1B visa holders boost American productivity, even if it has long been a source of controversy that has garnered bipartisan calls for reform.

“It’s going to have ripple effects throughout the whole economy,” said Jeremy Neufeld, the director of immigration policy at the Institute for Progress, a think tank focused on innovation.

Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement that Mr. Trump would continue to focus on growing the U.S. economy, and that there was “no shortage of American minds and hands to grow our labor force.”

Proponents of the administration said they welcomed the Trump administration’s attempts to prioritize American workers.

“Absolutely it is a positive step, and I would even say long overdue,” said Mark Krikorian, the executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, a think tank that favors lower immigration rates.

item.title: The 77-Year-Old Grandparents Accused of Killing Their Son-in-Law
item.description:
On a warm Saturday afternoon this fall, Jonathan McKinsey had just finished playing with his three children at a Bay Area park. He dragged a wagon past a baseball diamond and crowded playground and began to load items into the trunk of his SUV.

Then a bullet struck the back of his head, prosecutors say. Within 40 seconds, at least 17 more rounds were fired at Mr. McKinsey.

It was shocking enough that Mr. McKinsey was shot repeatedly in a park filled with children in Dublin, Calif., a Bay Area suburb popular among tech workers.

But the killing, on Sept. 26, reverberated far beyond Northern California after the authorities said the assailants were Mr. McKinsey’s 77-year-old in-laws. And headlines all over the world noted Mr. McKinsey’s role as director of engineering for the department at The New York Times that produces Wordle and other games.

Prosecutors say that the in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, jointly carried out a murder plot amid contentious divorce proceedings and a custody battle between Mr. McKinsey and their daughter, Candice Jang. Mr. McKinsey had been married to Ms. Jang for 15 years and had three children, with her before they were recently separated.

Defense lawyers have not disputed that the couple shot Mr. McKinsey, but say that they did so out of fear for their safety as well as the safety of their daughter and grandchildren. They cite child abuse allegations against Mr. McKinsey as well as the ongoing family court proceedings.

“The larger court record is replete with facts supporting both self-defense and defense of others,” Amy Cheng, a deputy public defender who represents Mr. Zhang, said in a recent filing.

The details of the allegations are laid out in court documents that have been unsealed or filed in recent weeks. Mr. Zhang, Ms. Chen and their lawyers could not be reached for comment. The Alameda County District Attorney’s office, which is prosecuting the case, said it would not comment on an ongoing case.

Both Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen have pleaded not guilty and are being held without bail. They are expected to return to court on Monday for a pretrial hearing.

Prosecutors say that they believe Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen planned the shooting, and the murder charge the couple faces includes a special circumstance of “lying in wait.”

Mr. Zhang typically got around by bicycle, prosecutors say, but he rented a car the day before the shooting. His wife of nearly half a century, Ms. Chen, was behind the wheel and wearing a wig as the couple drove to the park. They brought with them two loaded pistols, according to the documents.

The couple, prosecutors say, waited at the park for several minutes until Mr. McKinsey handed off the three children to their daughter, who drove off.

Then, just after 3 p.m. in the Dublin Sports Grounds parking lot, Mr. Zhang shot Mr. McKinsey once in the back of the head, causing him to fall to the ground, police say. Mr. Zhang continued to fire at him while he lay motionless, according to footage captured by a school camera across the street that was cited by prosecutors and defense lawyers.

Seconds later, Ms. Chen left the vehicle and fired a second gun several times at Mr. McKinsey, who remained on the ground, prosecutors say. Mr. Zhang fired at him again, and the couple stared down at Mr. McKinsey, prosecutors said.

After the shooting, detectives found four photo albums in the Dublin apartment where Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen live. Mr. McKinsey’s face cut out of some of the pictures. On one photo, there were black ink marks on his chest and over his right eye, the very places he was later shot, prosecutors say.

After his arrest, Mr. Zhang was interviewed by the police, through a Mandarin interpreter. According to court documents, Mr. Zhang told the police that he had been thinking about killing Mr. McKinsey all day and that he had rented the car so he could drive to a gun range and practice shooting.

Mr. Zhang, a retired metallurgist, immigrated to Albuquerque from China in 1985. He was joined three years later by his wife and daughter. In 2016, he and his wife relocated to Northern California to be closer to their daughter and her family.

Years later, at the time of the shooting, Mr. Zhang believed that Mr. McKinsey had a “dark soul” and had treated his grandchildren poorly, including physical abuse, he told the police, according to court documents. He also believed his son-in-law had wanted to harm him.

Mr. McKinsey and his wife, Ms. Jang, 46, had each accused each other of verbal, physical and psychological abuse, according to previous court records. Mr. McKinsey was a transgender man and had accused Ms. Jang and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity.

Katharine Tinto, a clinical law professor at the University of California, Irvine, said the outcome of the case could hinge on the defendants’ state of mind during the killing.

Mr. Zhang was diagnosed with memory loss last year, his lawyers said. Ms. Chen’s lawyer said that Mr. Zhang was “in the grips of serious mental deterioration” and becoming increasingly paranoid about Mr. McKinsey.

Those factors or a self-defense argument could throw into question the proof of advanced planning required for a murder conviction, Ms. Tinto said.

“That’s what the heart of this case seems to be: how culpable are these parents, and what was their intention, what was their mental state when they did these acts?” she said.

Mr. Zhang told detectives that he told his wife to drive them to the park and to bring a gun, but that she did not know anything more. They did not discuss killing Mr. McKinsey, Mr. Zhang told detectives.

Ms. Chen’s attorney, Curtis Briggs, wrote in a recent court filing that Ms. Chen could not see clearly what was happening from the driver’s seat of the car when Mr. Zhang was shooting at Mr. McKinsey. She saw what appeared to be her husband doubled over in pain clutching his abdomen, and rushed out to protect him from what she feared was an assault from a “violent and dangerous Mr. McKinsey,” Mr. Briggs said.

But prosecutors argue that Ms. Chen knew of her husband’s plan because she brought a firearm and wore a black wig to cover her normally silver hair.

It remains unclear what, if anything, Ms. Jang knew about their plans. Investigators have searched her home, but she has not been charged with a crime. She declined to be interviewed when reached by phone.

On a recorded jail-line call between Ms. Jang and Ms. Chen, Ms. Chen asked her daughter to return the rental car so that it didn’t accumulate late fees, according to Mr. Briggs’ court filings.

She told her repeatedly to take good care of the children. And, according to the filings, she apologized for “all the stress I’m causing you.”

Amy Qin contributed reporting.

item.title: A Chicago Park Is Infested With Rats. Is a Wealthy Couple to Blame?
item.description:
They carry satchels filled with nuts. They appear in Chicago’s Lincoln Park at all hours. And, according to some who have confronted them, they do not respond kindly to criticism.

For months, one of Chicago’s fanciest neighborhoods and one of its most beloved parks have been overcome by dual incursions of rats and nut-spreading strangers. Holes leading to subterranean rodent dens have sullied once-pristine parkland. Residents have cut back on picnics and stopped allowing their children to go barefoot.

Many believe they know who to blame: the wealthy household down the street.

Long before nut distribution became a regular occurrence in Lincoln Park, neighbors of Barre Seid, who in 2021 donated more $1.6 billion to a political nonprofit that backs conservative causes and candidates, had complained to city officials about animal-feeding outside the couple’s sleek but unassuming nearby house.

They claimed that his wife, Barbara Seid, would leave nuts on a terrace separating their property from a small public plaza. Squirrels and pigeons came to feast, they told the authorities — and rats followed.

Timmy Knudsen, who represents the area on the City Council, said his ward had long struggled with rats. When neighbors complained about the wildlife feeding at the Seids’ house, he said, officials repeatedly tried to address the problem, first with friendly letters, then with citations. Inspectors were dispatched to the property dozens of times, he said. Twice, city records show, Mr. Seid was issued tickets with penalties of $300 to $600.

Nothing worked.

“This letter is a FINAL WARNING,” Mr. Knudsen wrote on official letterhead to Mr. Seid over the summer. He accused him of creating a “public health hazard” and threatened police involvement. He got no response.

To this day, the Seids’ side of the story remains unclear. Their property, situated in a walkable area abounding in Pilates studios and French eateries, is adorned with a colorful assortment of No Trespassing signs.

Several attempts to reach the couple for comment failed. Emails sent to a civic organization associated with Ms. Seid went unanswered, as did messages left on phone numbers linked to the couple. When a reporter standing in the adjacent public plaza told a woman in the home’s entryway that he was from The New York Times, she slammed the front door before a question could be asked.

Mr. Seid, who made his fortune in electronics manufacturing, is perhaps best known for the 2021 donation, which was believed to have been one of the largest gifts ever made to a politically-focused nonprofit organization.

Chicago is heavily Democratic, but Mr. Knudsen and the neighbors insisted that the complaints had nothing to do with the Mr. Seid’s conservative politics, nor did they suspect political motives for the nut-spreading. The most common hypothesis is that someone in the household just really loves squirrels.

In a brief statement, Chicago’s Department of Streets and Sanitation said it had linked people at the couple’s address to nut-spreading in Lincoln Park but did not believe the household was the main cause of the park’s rat problem. The department did not specify the basis for that claim.

Mr. Knudsen and many in the neighborhood are convinced that the Seids have dispatched people to the park with nut-filled satchels. And as the city’s official admonishments of the Seids mounted this year, residents’ complaints largely shifted to the park, where sightings of nut-spreaders increased.

In neighborhood group chats, Facebook posts and conversations at the farmers’ market, residents swapped sightings of the nut depositors. Some appeared around sunrise, when only the earliest-rising dog walkers were out. Others popped up in broad daylight, as the park teemed with stroller-pushers and joggers.

Witnesses described the spreaders — men and women, young and old — pulling nuts from bags slung over their shoulders, then placing them on and around trees.

Adrienne Eltink, who walks her dog in the park, said she had often seen spreaders. She described piles of nut shells forming at the bases of trees, along with large rat tunnels.

“It makes it so unpleasant if every morning you’re walking and you have to watch your step because you’re either going to step on a dead rat or you’re going to have a rat scurry over your feet,” Ms. Eltink said.

Whatever the source of the squirrels’ bounty, the opportunistic rat population has feasted on it.

“If we’re talking a large nut, that could be sufficient for one rat per day,” said Matt Frye, a rodent management specialist at Cornell University.

“The more you feed rats,” he added, “the more likely you are to breed them.”

Grossed-out park-goers are just one consequence of a booming rat population, Dr. Frye said. Rats can also carry diseases, damage infrastructure and harm the environment.

Caroline Novak said that on one occasion, she saw someone leave the Seids’ home with a satchel, then spread nuts inside the park.

When WGN-TV elevated the story from hyperlocal curiosity to citywide fascination, Ms. Novak became a neighborhood celebrity by describing the outdoor buffet as “a luxury mélange of really nice nuts.”

“I’m talking Brazil nuts and walnuts,” she told the TV station. “These are not acorns.”

Ms. Novak, a physician, told The Times that she started approaching the spreaders to ask what they were up to. Some were brusque but cordial. Others less so.

“I said, ‘Hey, why are you throwing those nuts under these trees?’” Ms. Novak said, recounting a run-in last month with a satchel-carrying man. The response, she said, was an expletive-accented version of “None of your business.”

Ms. Eltink described being given the middle finger and being shouted at by a nut spreader whom she confronted.

Mr. Knudsen said he alerted the Chicago Police Department about the nut-spreading, but he acknowledged in an interview that it did not seem to be a top police priority.

Police Department officials said there were no incident reports this year at the Seids’ address but did not comment further. Streets and Sanitation officials said they had repeatedly baited rats in the park and were testing “fumigation methods” in the area.

On a recent stroll through Lincoln Park — an iconic stretch of North Side green space that is home to a zoo, sports fields and sweeping views of Lake Michigan — Mr. Knudsen pointed out exotic-looking nut shells and rat holes in the ground.

“You can see these nuts — these aren’t natural to this area,” he said. “Even when you step, you just crunch on nuts.”

Within Chicago’s municipal hierarchy of needs, Mr. Knudsen allowed, unauthorized nuts in a well-to-do neighborhood were a relatively minor concern. This is, after all, a city with hundreds of homicides each year and major budget problems.

Still, real damage was being done to a park that has long been a Chicago jewel, he said. And as attempts to stop the feeding faltered, Mr. Knudsen was left pondering a more existential question.

“Who is above the law anymore,” Mr. Knudsen asked, when a person suspected of wrongdoing is “not afraid of any civil punishment? Can they just do whatever they want?”

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Tech Outages Are Only the Beginning. A.I. Will Bring More Disruptions.
item.description:
Sometimes, especially lately, it can seem like computer software is built on a house of cards.

That is how the cybersecurity researcher Paulos Yibelo felt when he discovered a vulnerability in document and image processing software that is ubiquitous across the internet. The bug he found, called Upload2Shell, would enable a hacker to break into Google, Zoom and potentially thousands of other companies’ software just by uploading a file.

Mr. Yibelo, who recently founded a company called PWN AI, unearthed the bug by using artificial intelligence to meticulously probe what happens behind the scenes when people upload files to different services. He found that Ghostscript, software initially created 38 years ago to convert images to different formats, could be exploited by uploading files containing a custom font to execute malicious computer code. Mr. Yibelo reported the flaw to Artifex, the Ghostscript developer, and affected companies, which issued patches.

Mr. Yibelo’s finding, which has not been previously reported, is another example of how advanced A.I. has in a matter of months radically transformed cybersecurity and plunged the world into a disorienting new digital chapter in which severe technological disruptions may become far more commonplace than they were in the past, according to current and former U.S. and Western intelligence officials, security engineers and A.I. experts.

Those tremors have now bled into the daily life of Americans, as their email inboxes go dark and their flights are grounded. Viral rumors on social media have stoked confusion and fear about a widespread internet outage that could affect banking systems or critical infrastructure, even if recent events were not all A.I. related. It’s impossible for average people to tell what’s a malicious hack — could, for example, a 401(k) be drained? — and what’s simply antiquated software.

Over the past two weeks, a flood of outages slowed banking transactions, disrupted Microsoft products, interrupted Apple services, shut down a key system at the National Security Agency and temporarily grounded all commercial air traffic in the United States.

Officials have said they had no evidence that those episodes were caused by malicious cyberattacks. Instead, for a number of the outages, aside from the national air grounding, U.S. officials pointed to a more mundane explanation: Companies and government agencies are hardening their digital systems against new vulnerabilities, and these software patches are going awry.

In some of those episodes, including at the National Security Agency, the vulnerabilities at issue were detected with the help of A.I., according to U.S. officials. Individuals and businesses alike are using A.I. models to easily spot overlooked computer bugs and, in some cases, build proof-of-concept hacks in days or even hours that once might have taken scores of elite teams months to assemble.

At the same time, fears that bad actors are also using A.I. to work just as quickly have made defenders feel like they need to sprint to push fixes, which can result in messier updates that lead to disruptions.

Events last month were considered so alarming that some cybersecurity doomsayers (and opportunity-seeking marketing specialists) took to referring to the month as “Black October.” The label conveyed a sense that the world appeared to be suffering through a never-ending cascade of A.I.-powered software vulnerabilities that left defenders outmanned and exhausted.

The gloom has been even worse this month, putting a public already anxious about technology’s rapid pace of acceleration further on edge.

It is unlikely to be a momentary blip.

Estimates vary, but cybersecurity experts have said that the next year or two could be especially perilous, as advanced A.I. models find coding bugs that humans never spotted before — even if many malicious hacks remain more mundane. Some hope that after that painful transition period the internet will reach an equilibrium as A.I. helps overwrite vulnerable computer code. Others hold the more jaundiced view that A.I. represents an interminable threat to the interconnected technology upon which modern life and the global economy operate.

The past week is “the new normal,” retired Gen. Paul M. Nakasone, the former head of the N.S.A. and U.S. Cyber Command, said at a conference held in Washington by Vanderbilt University’s Institute of National Security.

“Industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize and at the same time defend themselves,” Mr. Nakasone said. “A.I. is driving all of this — the opportunities and the challenges.”

Mr. Nakasone, who is an OpenAI board member, described A.I. as “the most disruptive technology” in history, which would have profound consequences not just for the digital world but also the rest of society. “We are in an era where we’ve got to think differently about how we’re going to be more resilient.”

Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, is credited with popularizing the Silicon Valley cri de coeur to “move fast and break things.” A more honest assessment of the internet might be that it was broken from the start, and moved too fast to ever be fixed.

The rise of the technology industry has been defined by fierce competition, as companies jockeyed to rush their products to consumers quickly while security, which can create friction and slow progress, often remained an afterthought. Deficiencies in hasty code build over time, a concept known as technical debt. The focus on rapid product development has left many tech products riddled with hidden security holes that, at least historically, only a few determined hackers might find and exploit.

“The amount of technical debt that most companies will allow and live with is unforgivable,” said Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade, a distinguished fellow for security and A.I. research at the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. “Folks have been riding until the wheels fall off when it comes to technology. There’s always money in releasing, and there’s no money in maintaining.”

A.I. has upended the playing field, making it much easier to find the cracks in popular software. New cyber-focused A.I. models that can ferret out vulnerabilities have whipped some bug hunters into a frenzy as they compete to find novel ways to break into systems. Companies have also bought in, using A.I. to blast their own infrastructure and find bugs before hackers can.

“You’re essentially taking these brittle code bases and shaking them,” Mr. Guerrero-Saade said.

Even the N.S.A., which specializes in hacking and cyberdefense, is not immune. It had a days-long classified network outage this week because it installed faulty updates that sought to address flaws in the PHP programming language that were uncovered by A.I.-wielding researchers, officials said.

This week, Senator Maria Cantwell of Washington, the senior Democrat on the commerce committee, and Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota, the Republican chairman of a cybersecurity subcommittee, wrote a letter to the White House warning that A.I.-enabled cyber threats were outmaneuvering America’s defense systems.

“A.I. is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” the senators wrote in a letter to Jay Clayton, the national intelligence director, who also leads the White House super intelligence task force. “We cannot meet these threats with yesterday’s cybersecurity infrastructure or rely on individual companies to solve a problem that spans the entire digital economy.”

Recent data shows just how dramatically A.I. is transforming the cybersecurity ecosystem. Microsoft released over 1,400 patches for its various products last month, a rate about 10 times higher than its historic baseline. The tally eclipsed the previous record of nearly 1,000 set just a month earlier, in September.

Experts worry that there are fewer qualified humans available to triage the bug explosion. Major tech companies have made mass layoffs this year, in part because they have sought to replace workers with A.I., leaving them without institutional knowledge about how their old code was written.

New hiring data released this week by LinkedIn and reviewed by The New York Times showed that despite the rise in cybersecurity incidents and more bugs spotted than ever, U.S. cybersecurity hiring has underperformed relative to overall hiring.

Lea Kissner, the chief information security officer at LinkedIn, said that the current cybersecurity challenges meant companies needed humans with expertise more than ever.

“No one knows the best way to do security right now, because everything is changing so quickly,” said Dr. Kissner. “So you desperately need people who understand how things work, and have curiosity, and know how to solve problems.”

Despite the deluge of bugs exposed by A.I., some things haven’t changed. Most recent major cyberattacks have demonstrated hackers don’t need A.I., or only use it on the margins, to achieve their goals.

Iran’s targeting of scores of municipal water systems in the United States this summer largely relied on rudimentary tactics that seized on weak or default passwords on the computers that control operations. A criminal group’s hack of the F.B.I.’s sensitive personnel files relied on unpatched Oracle software that had been available for months. And recent attacks on refrigeration systems in Europe also appear to be relatively unsophisticated.

Of the 1,400 bugs identified last month by Microsoft, only one was something that was already weaponized by hackers, as the security journalist Brian Krebs observed. The gap reflects that for all the fear around A.I. most cyberattacks are still rooted in people not addressing basic, longstanding problems or patching known bugs.

Michael Yeh, Microsoft’s vice president of customer security and trust, said in a recent interview that over the past year, the top five bugs Microsoft was seeing used by hackers were exploits identified with patches three to six years ago.

“None of those are A.I.-driven attacks.” Mr. Yeh said. “These are people exploiting existing legacy vulnerabilities” that can be decades old. The failure to address age-old problems remained a bigger threat today than A.I., Mr. Yeh said. “And so I think they have to be eyes wide open about that.”

Some security experts believe A.I. is ushering in an era of more resilient online systems. They predict a future in which A.I. has eradicated technical debt and systems are far more secure. But others believe that the cycle of bug-finding and patching will continue endlessly, as A.I. systems improve and find more complex flaws.

Rob Joyce, the former top cybersecurity official at the N.S.A., said that A.I. was not “inventing brand new ways to hack” but instead applying more pressure on the need to fix existing problems — while offering a potential way forward.

Speaking Friday at Cyberwarcon, an annual gathering of security experts outside Washington, D.C., Mr. Joyce likened the current situation to a forest fire.

“All that tech that’s on fire and going to burn down, and on the other side of it, all the little things that are down in the forest floor, they’re going to grow,” Mr. Joyce said during a conference keynote. “They’re going to be stronger. They’re going to be more capable. But we’ve got to live through this era where stuff’s on fire.”

Mr. Yibelo, the PWN AI researcher, said he was skeptical that a smoother road was ahead because the newer, stronger models would continue to be capable of finding new flaws, including potentially in code fully written by earlier generations of A.I.

“I don’t know why there would be an end to the bugs,” Mr. Yibelo said. “It’ll always maybe be a cat-and-mouse game.”

item.title: 2-Year-Old Girl Wearing Only a Diaper Is Rescued After Hours in the Desert
item.description:
Jay Stewart walked through the Arizona desert on Wednesday with a flashlight to cut through the early morning darkness, searching for a missing 2-year-old girl who was last seen wearing only a diaper.

Two helicopters, dozens of vehicles, K-9 units and more than 100 people on the ground fanned out on Tuesday night in a remote part of Pinal County, Ariz., teeming with bushes and cactuses.

Drones looked for heat signatures as temperatures dropped to 45 degrees.

Mr. Stewart, a neighbor and volunteer search party member, said during a news conference on Wednesday that he saw coyote tracks and then heard the sounds of the animals in the distance as he trekked through the desert.

That was “a little disheartening,” he said. “They can definitely do some harm to a baby.”

Samuel Salzwedel, a spokesman for the Pinal County Sheriff’s Office, said that the child, Vella Campillo, had crawled through a fence around 5 p.m. and wandered from her home near Eloy, Ariz., which is about 50 miles northwest of Tucson.

Mr. Stewart looked over a ditch that was about three feet deep, which would be huge for a toddler, he said, and shined his flashlight around the brush.

“I’m calling her name — Vella, Vella — and behind me, to my left, I hear something that doesn’t even sound human,” Mr. Stewart said. “It was probably relief or fright.”

“She was in this bush, and she looked like she was swimming, kind of in this big bush,” he added at the news conference.

Mr. Stewart picked up Vella and tucked her into his flannel jacket for warmth. She clung to him, he said, and refused to let go.

In a video posted to the sheriff’s Facebook page on Wednesday, Mr. Stewart called the experience “a life-changing moment.”

Body camera footage from 12:22 a.m. on Wednesday shows Mr. Stewart holding Vella as he meets other rescuers.

In the video, Vella is vocal and clings to Mr. Stewart’s shirt as a responder places a blanket over her.

A sergeant can be heard in the footage saying that Vella did not have hypothermia. Mr. Salzwedel said on Saturday that Vella was taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. “We have no reason to believe she has any significant injuries,” he said.

He said that Vella had been found about two miles from her home.

Vella’s parents, Deanna Fritz and Joseph Campillo, told Fox10 Phoenix, a local television station, that Vella was playing with her siblings when she ran away while under the care of another family member.

Vella’s parents searched for her for about an hour before calling 911, Mr. Salzwedel said. Vella’s parents and Mr. Stewart did not respond to requests for comment on Saturday.

Sheriff Ross Teeple of Pinal County said during the news conference that the child’s size — Vella is about 25 pounds — added an extra challenge to the search.

“Very remote areas like this can get extremely cold very fast, and she’s a small body producing very little heat, so the drones with the heat signatures could not pick up anything,” he said.

Sheriff Teeple awarded Mr. Stewart a certificate of recognition, and an emblem that named him an honorary search-and-rescue posse member.

“I’ve never wanted to find something so bad in my life,” Mr. Stewart said at the news conference. “Or somebody to find her, anybody to find her. And it just happened to be me.”

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Trump Moves to Restrict Congressional Oversight of Contractors
item.description:
President Trump has directed federal contractors to seek permission from the White House before complying with congressional requests for information, the latest effort by the administration to blunt Democratic investigative plans next year.

In an executive order issued on Friday, Mr. Trump ordered contractors and subcontractors to coordinate responses to congressional queries with the White House, and to withhold information that the administration deems confidential or protected under “executive privilege.” Firms that fail to comply could have their contracts suspended or terminated, according to the order.

“The ability of the Congress to seek executive branch information is limited,” the order states. “It cannot seek information from executive branch departments and agencies, employees or federal contractors without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core executive functions.”

The move comes as Democrats, who will take control of the House and Senate next year, plan to cast a wide net in investigating everything from the administration’s policiesto any conflicts of interest it has had. This week, Representative Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, sent a dozen notices to members of Mr. Trump’s family, Vice President JD Vance and other current and former administration officials asking them to preserve documents on a host of issues.

Democrats have made clear that they intend to investigate no-bid contracts, and how alleged pay-to-play schemes might have influenced contracting decisions

Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat expected to lead the Judiciary Committee, called the order “blatantly unlawful.”

And Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who is poised to be the chairwoman of the Homeland Security Committee, said in her own statement that “every federal contractor should know that this executive order does not override their obligation to comply with congressional requests for information or subpoenas.”

She added: “Congress will get the information that it needs, and, if necessary, we will use every authority available to us to get it.”

The White House is mounting a combative response, seeking on several fronts to shield top officials, donors and members of Mr. Trump’s family.

Will Scharf, the White House counsel, sent a letter to Democrats on congressional committees saying that the White House would not respond to oversight requests until they took control of Congress in January. The White House has also maintained that congressional investigations “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” though it declined to say how. Legal experts have called the assessment dubious.

Mr. Trump, who has made retribution against his political enemies a priority of his second term, wrote in a social media post earlier this month that Democrats were engaging in “weaponization and lawfare at another level.” He added that “threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat political leaders,” and that he was directing the Justice Department to investigate the letters as “a criminal act.”

A fact sheet released by the White House outlined the new executive order’s goal as “protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach.” It accused some congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government,” in their efforts to intrude on “executive prerogatives.”

“The executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without concern that confidential information may be released to unauthorized third parties, even by federal contractors from a congressional request,” the fact sheet read.

Government watchdog groups said that the president’s order was an effort to cover up the widespread abuse of the contracting process over the last two years, including lucrative contracts that had been doled out to political allies and unqualified bidders.

“Contractors are paid with Americans’ tax money and must be the best for the job — full stop,” Lisa Gilbert, a co-president of the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said in a statement.

The order, she added, was “dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies,” and was “nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption.”

“It will not succeed,” Ms. Gilbert said.

item.title: Like Fiona the Hippo, Internet Famous Animals Can Bring Value to Zoos
item.description:
You might go your whole life and never come face to face with a hippopotamus. Or a sea otter. Or a tiger.

Social media, however, has a way of making the unknown known. And for many people, it helps create an emotional attachment to animals they have never seen in real life.

Fiona, a hippo at the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden, became an internet celebrity in 2017 after being born prematurely and beating the odds. The massive semiaquatic mammal died this week after eating a child’s hat that fell into her enclosure.

Fiona’s death prompted an outpouring of grief and fond memories from fans across the world who had fallen in love with the giant, big-toothed creature — even though many had never visited the zoo.

The internet has long been a place for animal videos to go viral, drawing thousands, if not millions, of views. Jimothy, the raccoon with a spinal condition in Seattle, became an online sensation.

For zoos, however, internet fame like Fiona’s offers not just a chance for clicks and likes, but a way to increase visitors, raise funds and bring awareness to critical issues. To be sure, there is a darker side of fame, especially when things go wrong. In recent days, commenters on social media have been calling for investigations into Fiona’s death — and justice.

Still, creating a following for zoo animals on social media is largely seen as beneficial and educational.

Viral critters serve as “ambassadors for their species,” said Liz MacDonald, the content strategy director at the Monterey Bay Aquarium in California. They spread joy but also can teach fans about conservation struggles that specific animals are facing, she added.

Take sea otters, the only fully aquatic otter species. They were facing extinction after being hunted for their fur in the 20th century. For years, the Monterey aquarium has offered a livestream of its sea otters, allowing viewers to delight in watching the cute, fuzzy creatures splash around.

While sea otters remain endangered, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the aquarium and its rehabilitation program for pups has helped a nearby estuary thrive despite the species’ global status.

One sea otter, Rosa, became a YouTube star.

Rosa was rescued by the Monterey Bay Aquarium as an orphaned baby in 1999, nursed to health and released into the wild. The aquarium kept tabs on Rosa, and she later returned to live out her later years at the aquarium after being deemed unfit to survive in the wild. In captivity, she acted as a surrogate mother to more than a dozen otters.

A YouTuber took a shine to Rosa and held an online fund-raiser on her birthday in 2019. The first year, the event raised a few hundred dollars in donations for the aquarium. Over the next few years, the total would break $1 million, Ms. MacDonald said.

“People really did connect with Rosa and her important work in terms of the recovery of her species,” Ms. MacDonald explained. “The online fans knew how many pups she raised. They understood the important role she played.”

Rosa died in 2024. She was 24, having well exceeded the typical life expectancy for her species, the aquarium said at the time.

Ms. MacDonald said that research had shown that bonds formed through social media can be effective far longer than a quick attention grab.

“When people feel a level of empathy with an animal that actually leads them to be more likely to have a pro-environmental identity and take pro-environmental behaviors,” Ms. MacDonald said. Techniques for helping to foster that empathy include giving animals human names and helping people understand their distinct personalities.

At the Bronx Zoo in New York City, visitors clamored to see Nadia, a tiger, when the zoo reopened following the Covid pandemic.

Nadia had contracted and survived a mild case of the virus in April 2020. While stuck at home, fans followed along with Nadia’s health journey online, said Craig Piper, the executive vice president of zoos and aquariums for the Wildlife Conservation Society.

“We’d have people asking, ‘How’s Nadia doing? Can we come see Nadia?’” Mr. Piper said. “There was a real surge in interest in people asking how to help tiger conservation.”

Tim Morrow, the chief executive at the San Antonio Zoo, said social media could help drive foot traffic and other financial opportunities.

The San Antonio Zoo began selling T-shirts after people became fond of Kevin, a wild duck who was living in a hippo enclosure. Timothy, one of the zoo’s hippos, found more fans online in 2018 after his keepers began penning and posting a series love letters from him to Fiona in Cincinnati.

The cutesy posts were also meant to be a teachable moment, Mr. Morrow explained.

As Timothy — or at least his social media mangers — wrote about wanting to visit Fiona, readers were actually learning about the ways zoos move animals around for breeding and species survival, Mr. Morrow said. The zoo saw a jump in visitors who were excited to meet Fiona’s long-distance boyfriend.

Michelle Curley, a spokeswoman for Fiona’s home zoo, declined to be interviewed.

This week, there was a final letter to Fiona.

“I may never have said ‘I love you,’ but please know I did. We all did,” the note read.

Once again, visitors have flocked to the zoo, Mr. Morrow said.

“What we try to do is create that spark because ultimately our mission is securing a future for wildlife, and we want the planet better. We want better for our animals,” he said. “These moments help really create that connection.”

item.title: Bigfoot Left a Paper Trail That Everyone Can See Now
item.description:
Many have tried — and failed — to confirm that Bigfoot, the folkloric apelike giant who is said to roam North America, is real. There have been reports of near misses, giant footprints and unexplained figures dotting the woods. But despite all efforts, the hairy biped has largely remained the stuff of campfire stories.

Last month, the federal government published records that some believers said bolstered the efforts to verify the creature’s existence.

The U.S. Forest Service has released a small set of documents pertaining to Bigfoot, who is also known as sasquatch in some Indigenous legends.

The documents included a 23-year-old newspaper article about mysterious tracks found in Montana, an Agriculture Department track report from Umatilla National Forest in Oregon from 1982 and a recounting of another track sighting in Montana in the 1940s.

The agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail,” a researcher, Rodney Johnson, wrote in the agriculture report, describing photos of large tracks he concluded had been “made by something other than a 300-pound-plus two-footed being.”

Bigfoot is largely believed to by mythical, but enough people have claimed to see the bipedal creature that the government has kept records.

For some, the content was not revelatory.

David Daegling is an anthropology professor at the University of Florida and the author of a 2004 book about Bigfoot’s legacy in the United States. “The file drop is not groundbreaking in the least,” he said in an email, describing the documents as “standard Bigfoot fare.”

Part of Bigfoot’s enduring mythos is that its qualities are amorphous, Mr. Daegling wrote in a 2019 article. Bigfoot is generally accepted as being “big, hairy and bipedal,” but beyond that, its characteristics are up for debate.

“Bigfoot’s ambiguity enables it to stay relevant,” he wrote. “It serves us well as a monster when we need that escape, and it just as easily can stand in for as an imperturbable guardian of the wilderness.”

Still, for those in the Bigfoot community, even the existence of the government-issued documents can feel like a legitimization.

These are not the first documents the Trump administration has released that are related to unexplained sightings.

This year, the Pentagon released records pertaining to U.F.O.’s, or “unidentified anomalous phenomena” as they are called officially. One document detailed a mysterious potato-esque object seen in the Colorado skies. (The government has suggested is was a trick of the light scattering off the snowy ground causing an optical illusion.)

Rick Foss, a board member of the North American Wood Ape Conservancy, a volunteer group devoted to the search for Bigfoot, was heartened by the new documents, which he said echoed the experiences and encounters of many of the conservancy’s members.

“This is something that hundreds and thousands of people have documented all throughout the country and the world, but we don’t hear about it from official sources,” Dr. Foss, who lives in Florence, Ariz., said. “It was nice to see it in a positive or a neutral light. It wasn’t being made fun of.”

His curiosity about Bigfoot was piqued as a child after watching “The Legend of Boggy Creek,” a docudrama about a large, hairy creature said to roam the swamps of Arkansas.

Dr. Foss, who is a counselor with a doctorate in forensic psychology, said that he had never had a Bigfoot sighting but that he believed that he had experienced a few close encounters. Those included hearing unidentifiable noises in the woods and hearing something slapping the side of his cabin in the early morning.

Bigfoot is never far from the cultural conversation in the United States.

Marq Evans, director of the 2026 documentary “Capturing Bigfoot,” said the elusive cryptid was “America’s favorite mystery.” In his film, Mr. Evans revealed that the most famed Bigfoot footage, the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film, appeared to have been an effective hoax. Believers and deniers alike have pored over that clip with a Zapruder-like intensity for years.

There are a few reasons people continue to get hooked on the hunt for Bigfoot, Mr. Evans said.

There’s the thrill of the unknown and a hunger for mystery “in a world that is mapped out and where we know almost everything,” he said. He also attributed the perpetual search to “frontier nostalgia” and the human desire to explore. Also, roaming the woods with friends is not a bad way to spend a day, he said with a laugh.

Jeremiah Byron, host of “Bigfoot Society,” a podcast, said the documents had made him hopeful that there would be more to come.

“They’re not saying Bigfoot is real, but they’re releasing documents that have to do with Bigfoot,” Mr. Byron, who is 43 and lives in central Iowa, said. “But this stuff is getting put out there by the government. What is going to come down the line next?”

item.title: The Penny Is Dead. Now It’s Official.
item.description:
Though the humble penny’s demise was declared a year ago, after President Trump sought an end to its run as a unit of U.S. currency, it was never quite legally laid to rest — until now.

On Friday, Mr. Trump signed into law the Common Cents Act, officially ending production of the one-cent coin that cost nearly four cents to mint. The act passed in September with no opposition in either the House or Senate.

Representative Lisa McClain, Republican of Michigan, one of the bill’s sponsors, noted in a statement that the outsize cost of minting pennies was a sign that “something is broken.” One of her co-sponsors, Senator Cynthia Lummis, Republican of Wyoming, also released a statement, saying, “We have modernized our coinage for the future.”

The law officially directs the Treasury Department to halt its minting of the penny, save for special collector coins. But the cessation of its production already came to pass on Nov. 12, 2025. On that day, the U.S. Mint stamped the last of its pennies at a special ceremony held in the place of the coin’s 1793 birth, Philadelphia. Three-coin collector sets — 232 total, one for each year the penny remained in production — were made to mark its end. Each set contained one penny made of 24-karat gold.

For decades, lawmakers have pushed for retiring the penny, motivated mostly by the coin’s inconvenience. In 1989, when there was legislation to get rid of it, The New York Times wrote that the penny was seen as “anachronistic and a nuisance,” and even panhandlers turned it away.

Lobbyists for the zinc industry fought back. The cost of producing the penny did not rise past its value until about a decade ago, according to the Treasury.

Mr. Trump’s plans to get rid of the penny, announced on Truth Social on Feb. 9, 2025, broke through that stalemate.

“For far too long the United States has minted pennies which literally cost us more than 2 cents,” he wrote. “This is so wasteful!”

The roughly 114 billion pennies in existence, the Treasury Department wrote in online guidance, would circulate “for as long as possible.” How long that might be would largely depend on “consumer behavior.” The Treasury guidance encouraged businesses to round up or down to the nearest five cents — only on cash transactions — and sought to assuage consumers’ concerns about rising costs by noting that the rounding would average out. The federal cost savings, the Treasury estimated, would be $56 million annually.

The new act formalizes that rounding guidance. It also paves the way for cheaper materials in minting the nickel, which costs nearly 14 cents to make.

If the nickel goes the way of the penny, some collectors may rejoice. On Dec. 11, 2025, the 232 sets of collector pennies sold for a total of $16.76 million at an auction hosted on behalf of the U.S. Mint. The final set of three, containing the very last pennies stamped, sold for $800,000.

item.title: Judge Blocks Trump Administration’s Effort to Transform Homelessness Policy
item.description:
The Trump administration’s battle to transform homelessness policy suffered a new setback on Friday when a federal judge blocked its latest effort to shift funding from housing aid to programs that require treatment for mental health or addiction.

The ruling came shortly before the administration was set to announce thousands of grants to nonprofit groups, and barred it from steering much of the annual funding to the treatment-centered efforts it favors. Since the treatment money would have come from existing housing programs, critics said large numbers of formerly homeless people risked being evicted.

The ruling is the third time that Mary S. McElroy, a federal judge in Rhode Island, has blocked the government’s efforts to rewrite grant-making rules that control billions of dollars in annual aid. In reserving about a third of the funding, $1.3 billion, for treatment programs, the administration “exceeded its statutory authority,” she wrote.

With current funding about to expire and service providers awaiting decisions, Judge McElroy gave the Department of Housing and Urban Development just five days to submit a new plan for disbursing the aid.

Ann Oliva, the chief executive officer of the National Alliance to End Homelessness, one of the groups that sued the administration, estimated that 97,000 formerly homeless people could have returned to the streets if the housing money had been redirected to treatment programs.

“On behalf of communities across the nation working to address homelessness, we applaud this decision,” she said. “The core of this fight is about the effectiveness of permanent supportive housing. Safe and affordable housing ends people’s homelessness.”

Scott Turner, the housing secretary, warned in statement that the ruling “disrupts $4 billion for our most vulnerable, just days before funding awards were set to be made.” While he added that “our ‘Treatment First’ mission will not be deterred,” he did not say if the department would appeal.

The ruling is part of a battle over a policy known as Housing First, which provides the homeless long-term rental subsidies. It also offers them treatment for addiction or mental illness, without requiring them to accept it. The approach, which emerged several decades ago, once enjoyed bipartisan support. Studies show it generally succeeds in getting people off the street, though there is little consistent evidence that it improves mental or physical health. Critics say the housing is expensive and fails to address what they call the “root causes” of homelessness, like addiction or psychiatric disorders. They hold it responsible for the long-term growth in homelessness. While the Trump administration has tried to create treatment mandates, Judge McElroy has repeatedly ruled that its efforts violate statutory intent or procedural requirements. Since Congress created the program to provide housing, plaintiffs have argued, the housing department lacks the authority to remake it around treatment efforts.

In addition to blocking the effort to move $1.3 billion into treatment, Judge McElroy curtailed other changes the housing department had sought for the grant-making process.

Her order barred the department from punishing groups that participate in so-called harm reduction efforts, like safe injection sites. It also barred the agency from promoting “self-sufficiency” by penalizing programs that help people get Medicaid, food stamps and Supplemental Security Income.

Devon Kurtz of the conservative Cicero Institute, which opposes Housing First, denounced the ruling as “a brazenly political decision” that curtailed legitimate efforts to promote goals like cooperating with law enforcement and promoting self-reliance.

If the ruling stood, he said, it would constitute a “major setback” to the administration’s efforts to revamp homelessness policy. “I pray they appeal,” he said.

For frontline groups working with the homeless, the uncertainty over the funding rules has made a hard task harder.

“It’s incredibly disruptive,” said Vivian Wan, the chief executive officer of Abode Services, a California housing provider in eight Bay Area counties.

If the housing department succeeded in shifting the money into treatment programs, about 240 apartments the group operates for the homeless would have lost their funding, she said, potentially displacing many of the residents.

“It’s painful to wait for the courts — but not waiting for the courts would be far more harmful to the people we serve,” she said.

item.title: ICE Officers Arrest 2 Passengers Boarding a Flight at Seattle Airport
item.description:
Federal immigration officers on Saturday arrested two passengers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as they were boarding a flight, prompting outrage from airport officials, who called the incident “distressing.”

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said the officers were conducting an operation to detain an immigrant from Mexico who had overstayed his visa. “During the arrest other travelers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers — a federal crime and a felony,” ICE said in a statement. “One passenger hurled hot coffee on the officers.”

Officers also arrested that passenger, another immigrant from Mexico who ICE said had overstayed her visa, and the agency said she would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

The arrests occurred as passengers were boarding an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles on Saturday morning. A video that circulated on social media showed people yelling and pleading during a physical confrontation on a jetway.

“I’m outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities,” Gov. Bob Ferguson of Washington, a Democrat, said on social media.

In July, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration had started arresting foreign citizens with expired U.S. visas as they traveled through airports, a tactic that opened a vast new pool of people for deportation.

“ICE’s conduct across our country is putting people in harm’s way, undermining public trust, and stoking fear in our communities,” Representative Adam Smith, Democrat of Washington, said on social media.

The Port of Seattle, which operates the airport, and Alaska Airlines said they did not have advance knowledge of the immigration enforcement action.

“This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred,” the Port of Seattle said in a statement.

Alaska Airlines said it was “working to understand the circumstances surrounding what occurred, including whether the proper protocols were followed.”

item.title: Republicans Debate Why They Lost This Year, and Whether It Rhymes With Trump
item.description:
After a generational flogging in the midterms, Republicans are bracing for a sharp loss of power with little consensus on how to regain their footing.

Democrats swept them out of office on the back of a public fury that rivaled the post-Watergate backlash of the 1970s, winning 56 percent of the popular vote — a margin unparalleled in the modern era — and ending decades-long streaks of Republican dominance in Texas, Kansas, Mississippi and South Carolina.

Republicans are now in the early stages of the soul searching that is typical for a party after major election defeats. But for this Republican Party, that period of reflection is complicated by President Trump’s enduring dominance. A clear divide has already emerged between those who say he bears significant culpability for the midterm losses, and those who are unwilling to cast blame his way.

In interviews, nearly 20 Republican lawmakers, strategists and officials gave a wide range of explanations for what they called a “shellacking,” an “apocalypse” and a “wholesale repudiation” of the party. They cited inflation, off-base messaging, vulnerability to Democratic attacks about corruption, and overzealous immigration enforcement.

David Kochel, an Iowa Republican strategist, called the midterms “a rejection of the president,” adding that “it felt to me like a bit of a recall election — like, ‘We screwed up in 2024 and we’re going to try to fix it as best we can.’”

Other party strategists, commentators and departing lawmakers have also grown far more blunt about what they see as Mr. Trump’s political failings. Prominent right-leaning figures like Elon Musk, Stephen K. Bannon and Joe Rogan have distanced themselves from the president.

Ben Shapiro, a prominent conservative pundit who campaigned for Mr. Trump, told NPR this past week that voters this election “went in and they said: ‘I think that the Trump administration has basically stunk up the joint. Throw ’em out.’”

“And I think it was really that simple,” he added.

But many other Republicans have blamed Mr. Trump’s policies, like tariffs, without directly blaming him. Vice President JD Vance frustrated the president by attributing the defeats to the Iran war, perhaps his boss’s most politically consequential decision.

Mr. Trump’s allies in Republican leadership, including Speaker Mike Johnson, have also avoided criticizing him or even offering much explanation of what went wrong. House Republicans just elected a close Trump ally, Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, to be their next leader. And while Mr. Trump has acknowledged that he may have overstepped on immigration, on Friday he blamed lawmakers for failing to “get the things that I wanted passed.”

The party’s limited reckoning over the midterms foreshadows the coming battle over its direction now that Mr. Trump is a lame-duck president — and suggests that influential Republican figures may be reluctant to change course.

Republican elected officials and strategists broadly agree that the party focused too much on culture-war issues, like transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports, and too little on kitchen-table topics that could appeal to independents and swing voters.

Senator Ted Cruz, now set to become the only major statewide Republican official in Texas, said on his podcast days after the election that “too many Republican politicians seemed like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care” about Americans’ “very real pain.”

Representative Beth Van Duyne of Texas, a Trump ally who won re-election in a House district that swung less to the left than any other in the state, said in an interview that her colleagues had not talked enough about “meat-and-potato issues.” Representative Nathaniel Moran, a Texas Republican who also performed better than the top of the ticket, told The New York Times that “we became disconnected from the everyday, working-class man and woman and what was important to them at this moment.”

But the messaging problem was hard to untangle from the party’s actions. Many Republicans became increasingly vocal opponents of Mr. Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war, which were a major driver of cost increases, particularly for gas and diesel. And some aspects of Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy law also proved unpopular, notably its cuts to Medicaid benefits.

Senator Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican who is a potential 2028 presidential contender, said the election showed that his party must focus more on affordability issues and working-class voters.

“We’re a blue-collar state,” Mr. Hawley told The Associated Press this past week, referring to Missouri. “And I think the Republican Party will either be a blue-collar party or we will be a permanent minority party.”

In 2024, Mr. Trump campaigned on a promise to secure the border and deport immigrants who were in the country illegally. It worked.

But after this year’s rout, some Republicans have suggested that voters punished the party for the Trump administration’s aggressive tactics. Nationally, Hispanic voters shifted 31 percentage points to the left compared with the 2024 presidential election, according to Times Voter Trends, a larger change than for any other racial group.

Mr. Trump himself told CBS’s “60 Minutes” less than a week after the election that his deportation policy “might be too tough” and might have “hurt” Republican candidates.

Giancarlo Sopo, a Republican strategist who worked on two House campaigns in South Texas, said the immigration crackdown and high prices had supercharged turnout for Democrats and driven many Trump voters to turn on Republicans.

In 2024, Mr. Sopo said, Hispanic Americans “voted to make carne asada less expensive and to deport gang members,” not to see longtime neighbors locked up and sent away.

He added: “When you have masked agents showing up in sacred civic centers to pick people up, people are understandably indignant.”

At the same time, some hard-line Republicans — including Representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado, who lost her re-election bid — have said that the administration should have deported more people.

Mr. Trump has not indicated that he will change direction. Days after the election, he announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration agenda, would be his new chief of staff. The move raised political concerns even from some Trump allies.

“If your team takes a beating as badly as we took last week, you have to fire people,” Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana told CNN, calling Mr. Miller’s appointment a “mistake.”

Corruption was a top issue for voters this year, polls showed, a shift from previous elections.

The Republicans who have blamed concerns about self-dealing for the party’s losses include former Vice President Mike Pence and Senator John Cornyn of Texas, who lost his primary this year to Mr. Trump’s preferred candidate, the state attorney general, Ken Paxton.

Mr. Shapiro, the conservative commentator, told NPR that “the whiff of corruption surrounding the White House is truly awful.”

Former Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, a potential 2028 presidential candidate and a longtime Trump critic, said his party needed to demand higher standards of its leaders.

“We’ve taken a character holiday in the Republican Party for the last 10 years,” he said this month on the radio show “New Hampshire Today,” adding, “That lack of character has an impact on the country.”

The White House denied allegations of corruption, with a spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, saying that “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public — which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office.”

Republicans said they underestimated their opponents’ chances in states like Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Kansas, assuming decades of dominance would protect them.

In Texas, “we’ve been a one-party state for too long,” said Matt Mackowiak, a Republican strategist. “We got fat and happy.”

Ms. Van Duyne, the Texas congresswoman, said “Voters felt like they were taken for granted.”

Several said the party had focused too much on appeasing right-wing hard-liners.

“They think nothing is good enough, they think nothing is extreme enough,” said Representative Dan Crenshaw, who lost a Republican primary in March. “They think there’s not enough deportations.” He added that the party would “never win anything again” if it centered the hard-liners.

Republicans now face an uncertain leadership transition between Mr. Trump and the party’s eventual 2028 presidential nominee.

Few in the party have called for a new policy agenda, viewing the headwinds they faced in this year’s midterms as temporary or strictly related to messaging. Many are counting on Democrats to give them fodder for the campaign trail in two years by overreaching in oversight efforts or failing to deliver on their promises to lower costs.

An early indicator of Republicans’ direction will come in January, when the chair of the Republican National Committee, Joe Gruters, is up for re-election. Mr. Trump has already endorsed him, and a challenge from Mr. Gruters’s co-chair seems unlikely to succeed.

Frank Luntz, a longtime Republican pollster, had two words of advice for Republicans after the midterms: “Wake up.” He said that the party had ignored glaring red flags in the polls, and that Mr. Trump had gravely erred in telling voters that affordability was “a hoax.”

“Republicans need truth tellers,” Mr. Luntz said.

Others in the party are looking to history for answers.

“The Republican Party finds itself in a position that’s not unlike when we were coming out of ’06,” said Jimmy Centers, a Republican strategist in Iowa, referring to President George W. Bush’s midterm losses during the Iraq War.

He added, “It took the party roughly 10 years to figure it out.”

Shawn McCreesh contributed reporting.
